newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT - US bond futures bump channel resistance.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT - US bond futures bump channel resistance.

text.p: Technical analysts remained constructive on U.S. bond futures as the market saw a second day of robust gains and challenged resistance at the top of a two-month upward channel.

The high so far this session in the September contract corresponds roughly with the top of the channel, which follows the track of the May 13 high of 110-09, said Nick Kalivas, senior credit market analyst for Refco Inc.
The channel bottom is drawn off the April 11 low of 105-30 and May 27 low of 108-05.
September bond futures bumped up against the trendline barrier this morning, when they were turned back at the session high of 112-02, analysts said.
The contract was last at 111-24, up 12/32, after an initial rise on weaker than expected U.S. May producer prices. The overall and core indexes both fell 0.3 percent.

A bond futures floor analyst for a U.S. brokerage house said reluctance to gravitate far from yields of 6.75 percent in the cash bond and 6.00 percent in the two-year note also was limiting the upside in Treasurys. In futures terms, 6.75 percent equates to about 111-20, the analyst said.
Kalivas said his medium-term outlook for bonds was constructive, aimed at the mid-February highs.
September bond futures peaked at 113-09 on February 18.
"I would tend to maintain that outlook as long as we continue, on a weekly continuous basis, to close above 110-22," he said.
Kalivas said 6.00 percent on the two-year Treasury, at just 50 basis points above the federal funds target, was formidable psychological resistance for the market.
He said he was also wary of a potential bearish divergence in daily stochastics in the next few days, as the indicator has yet to confirm the recent rally.
Brad Tyl, bond floor analyst with Aubrey G. Lanston & Co., predicted the September bond would next test the 6.65 percent yield level, equal to about 112-24 in futures.

Bonds cut a wide swath between about 6.65 percent and 6.80 percent on February 26, the date of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins congressional testimony, creating a vacuum of resistance until 6.65 percent, Tyl said.
